name: Dyakonov's Physics Arguments
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: An Engineer's Case Against the Impossible Machine
lesson.summary: Michel Dyakonov, a condensed matter physicist, argues that quantum computing's obstacle is not a violation of physical law but an engineering demand without real precedent: reliably controlling an enormous number of coupled, continuously valued physical degrees of freedom well enough, for long enough, to run a useful algorithm.
lesson.body:
The chapter on the engineering versus physics barrier drew a distinction that recurs in discussions of ambitious technology: something can be fully permitted by the laws of physics and still be practically out of reach because of what building it requires in materials, precision, cost, and time. Michel Dyakonov, a condensed matter physicist with a long career studying real materials and devices, has argued for years, including in a widely discussed essay often cited under the title The Case Against Quantum Computing, that quantum computing sits on the engineering side of that line: not forbidden by physics, but demanding an engineering feat with no real precedent to reassure us it is achievable.

The core of his argument concerns scale and precision together. Useful fault-tolerant algorithms, the kind that would outperform classical computers on problems people care about, are generally estimated to need not dozens or hundreds but potentially millions of high quality physical qubits once error correction overhead is counted. Dyakonov's skepticism centers on whether any apparatus can reliably prepare, control, and read out that many coupled degrees of freedom, keeping them correctly related, for long enough to finish a useful computation. His point is not that any single qubit is impossible to build, labs build good qubits routinely, it is that the jump from dozens of qubits to millions may not be more of the same challenge at larger size, it may be a harder regime existing progress does not straightforwardly predict.

To make this concrete, Dyakonov draws an analogy to analog computing's history. Early computers, some genuinely useful, represented numbers with continuous quantities, voltages, mechanical positions, rather than digital encodings. Analog computers were largely abandoned for digital ones because continuous signals accumulate noise and drift with every operation, with no natural way to reset a corrupted value the way a digital circuit snaps a noisy voltage back to a clean zero or one. Dyakonov argues quantum states carry a related vulnerability: a quantum state is described by continuous complex amplitudes, not discrete symbols, and while quantum error correction is designed to fight exactly this fragility, a point the next chapter examines, his skepticism is that doing so reliably at useful scale is the same category of hard, continuous parameter control problem that sank large scale analog computing.

Dyakonov's claim is narrower than it is often summarized as: not that quantum mechanics breaks down at some qubit count, nor that a fault-tolerant quantum computer is impossible in principle, but that the engineering demands are severe enough that success within any useful timeframe or cost should not be assumed just because smaller demonstrations keep succeeding. This distinguishes his critique from Kalai's mathematical noise argument, and sets up the most concrete version of his concern, the sheer size of the parameter space a large quantum computer must control, which the next chapter examines directly.

Supporters of the mainstream roadmap respond with the field's own trend data: coherence times, gate fidelities, and qubit counts have improved substantially over two decades, evidence, they argue, that the challenge is tractable rather than blocked. Skeptics reply that a decade of improvement at tens or hundreds of qubits does not guarantee the same rate at millions, since new effects, cross talk, materials defects, control limits, may only dominate at scales not yet reached. This debate remains genuinely open.
